title: ThreeJS is underrated
author: Fun_Mission_6974
selftext:
Honestly, I think Three.js is pretty underrated when it comes to gaming.

People don’t realise how much you can actually do with it. You can make 3D games that run straight in the browser without needing people to download anything.

You can build environments, physics, lighting, animations, particle effects and even multiplayer games. And the fact that it all runs using JavaScript is pretty impressive.

Obviously, it’s not going to replace Unreal Engine or Unity for big AAA games, but I think people overlook how powerful it is for browser games and smaller indie projects.

I also think there’s a lot of potential for developers who want to experiment with game development without having to learn an entire game engine straight away.

It’s not perfect, and performance can be an issue with more complex games, but there’s genuinely a lot you can do with it.

I just think Three.js deserves way more attention in the gaming space than it gets.

comments.author: sunnystormy64
comments.body:
People don't understand the accessibility of three.js because most computer users are stuck in a "Wintel" mindset and don't ask any deep questions about software and hardware.

I opened up tickets about porting Godot to RISC-V and ARM64 a long time ago, and got a chilly reception back then. Today, I can develop three.js applications on my tablet, a RISC-V single-board computer, and so on.

I don't think there's any need to run a platform-dependent editor to build games. You'd only want a performant runtime when you're ready to distribute (which can be tailored to a target platform).

comments.author: NoMacJustMagic
comments.body:
Agree 100%. I'm building a mobile 3D RPG in Three.js right now: open world, gathering skills (woodcutting, mining), combat, and rebuilding a village. It runs straight in the phone browser, so testers can just tap a link and play.

The biggest surprise for me was how far you get with simple tricks: instancing for trees and rocks, baked lighting, and Mixamo animations through the GLTF pipeline. Performance on mobile is the real challenge. You have to watch draw calls and texture sizes from day one.

What it lacks compared to Unity is the editor and tooling, so you end up building your own. But no install, instant sharing and fast iteration make up for a lot.
